### GOVERNING THOUGHT
The cohort demonstrates foundational component implementation but struggles with architectural defense, first-principles reasoning, and token economy in LLM systems. Trainees often proceed with implementation without fully understanding underlying concepts, leading to inefficiencies and difficulty in addressing complex architectural challenges.

### KEY ARGUMENT 1 — Foundational Understanding vs. Implementation Depth
Trainees show an ability to implement basic components but lack a deep understanding of *why* certain architectural choices are made or *how* to optimize them at scale.

*   **Evidence of struggle with first principles:** Siddharth repeatedly emphasizes the need for trainees to understand concepts before implementing them. He notes, "unless and until you don't understand stuff, don't implement it. Okay, if you don't understand it, come and ask me, I'll explain it to you" [2026-07-22, Page 3-4 — Siddharth Saminathan]. This suggests a tendency to jump to implementation without full comprehension.
*   **Misunderstanding of core concepts in practice:** When Himaya attempts to implement caching, Siddharth questions her understanding of *why* caching was brought up and *what* she was asked to cache, indicating a disconnect between the instruction and its practical application [2026-07-22, Page 1-2 — Siddharth Saminathan].
*   **Emphasis on fundamental knowledge:** Siddharth stresses that "Caching, embeddings, how to, you know, save on embedding costs at scale. Those will be, these buttons will haunt you forever. As long as you are an AI engineer, in every interview they will ask you, okay? And it is so important to... Name the fundamentals here" [2026-07-22, Page 3-4 — Siddharth Saminathan]. This highlights a perceived gap in fundamental understanding among the trainees.

### KEY ARGUMENT 2 — Architectural Defense and Scalability Challenges
The cohort struggles to defend their architectural decisions, particularly when confronted with questions about scalability, cost optimization, and efficient resource utilization in production environments.

*   **Difficulty in defending RAG design:** Dakshinya initially struggles to explain why she is sending all 10 retrieved chunks to the LLM, even if only three are relevant. Siddharth presses her on the inefficiency and cost implications of sending "70,000 tokens... for every user" when only a fraction is relevant [2026-07-22, Page 10-11 — Siddharth Saminathan]. This demonstrates a lack of immediate consideration for token economy and efficiency in her RAG design.
*   **Lack of proactive cost optimization:** When asked about reducing embedding costs by 70% in a production scenario, Dakshinya's initial response is "database calls" before being guided back to caching and signal-to-noise ratio, indicating a reactive rather than proactive approach to cost-efficient architecture [2026-07-22, Page 13-14 — Siddharth Saminathan].
*   **Challenges in modularization and reusability:** Siddharth instructs Dakshinya to transform a single Python file into a modular, reusable Fast API architecture with clearly defined subsystems (parsing, cleaning, semantic chunking, embedding generation, vector store, RAG/retrieval service, prompt builder, context engineering engine, reusable re-ranker, LLM generation client, unified evaluation system). He emphasizes identifying "what needs to be reused, what doesn't need to be reused" [2026-08-17, Page 4-5 — Siddharth Saminathan]. This indicates that the initial designs lacked modularity and reusability, which are critical for scalable systems.
*   **Struggles with database integration for LLMs:** Ganesh's approach to handling Excel files by throwing away formatting to put data into a database for LLM access is questioned by Siddharth. Siddharth states, "I don't think this is the right way to do it. OK, I'm not sure whether your database will give you the exact Excel coordinates" [2026-07-14, Page 7-9 — Siddharth Saminathan]. This points to a challenge in designing robust data handling mechanisms for LLMs, especially concerning data integrity and specific access requirements.

### KEY ARGUMENT 3 — Token Economy and Context Window Management
Trainees frequently overlook the critical aspects of token economy and efficient context window management, leading to suboptimal performance and increased costs in LLM interactions.

*   **Inefficient token usage in RAG:** Siddharth highlights Dakshinya's default approach of sending all 10 retrieved chunks to the LLM, regardless of relevance. He states, "Do you still need to send those 70,000 tokens?... for every user?" [2026-07-22, Page 11-12 — Siddharth Saminathan]. This demonstrates a failure to optimize token usage, leading to unnecessary cost and latency. The solution involves re-ranking to send only relevant chunks [2026-07-22, Page 11-12 — Siddharth Saminathan].
*   **Misunderstanding of batch size and context window relationship:** Dakshinya incorrectly assumes the context window of DeepSeek and LLaMA models is the same. Siddharth corrects her, explaining that "When you're changing the context window, obviously you need to change your batch size because if your context window gets bigger, you can send more data in" [2026-07-29, Page 11 — Siddharth Saminathan]. This indicates a gap in understanding how model-specific parameters influence performance and efficiency.
*   **Need for context engineering:** Siddharth instructs Dakshinya to perform "context engineering" and "set and calculate, take the number of tokens from all the documents, the summary, take that, take those tokens" to efficiently use the 1 million context window, aiming for "30,000, 40,000 tokens of breathing room" [2026-08-07, Page 2-3 — Siddharth Saminathan]. This directly addresses the need for trainees to actively manage and engineer the context provided to LLMs, rather than simply batching.
*   **Impact of large data on token limits:** Ganesh's concern that passing a JSON of "thousands of... rows and columns right there in this so if we are passing the JSON file like JSON of thousands and all to directly to LLM will it be like it will be context heavy right and the tokens and all will be Very much" [2026-07-14, Page 7-9 — Ganesh Krishna] indicates an awareness of the problem but his proposed solution (throwing away structure into a database) reveals a struggle with finding an effective and architecturally sound solution.
